headline: 4D Gaussian Splatting Comes to the Browser via PlayCanvas
lede: A technique for rendering dynamic 3D scenes in real time — previously the domain of research labs and GPU clusters — has been integrated into an open-source web engine, putting photorealistic, time-varying scenes a browser tab away. The announcement, from a figure tied to the PlayCanvas project, pairs the engine with Gracia VR, a platform built around the format. It is a small but meaningful step in closing the gap between cutting-edge graphics research and everyday web delivery.
body:
**Gaussian splatting** is a rendering method that represents a scene not as polygons or a neural network but as a cloud of overlapping, semi-transparent ellipsoids — Gaussians — each carrying colour and opacity. Unlike mesh-based graphics, the representation is learned directly from photographs, and unlike earlier *neural radiance fields* (NeRFs), it renders in real time because the splats are rasterised rather than ray-marched through a network. The technique became a breakout result in computer graphics in 2023.

The "4D" extension, published at both ICLR 2024 and CVPR 2024 by separate research groups, adds time as a fourth dimension to those primitives. Each Gaussian is parameterised by an anisotropic ellipse that can rotate arbitrarily in space *and* time, with appearance encoded by 4D spherindrical harmonics — a mathematical basis that captures how colour changes across viewing angle and moment. The result is a compact representation of a dynamic scene — a person moving, cloth rippling, a car driving — from which novel views at any desired timestamp can be synthesised on the fly.

The practical challenge has been delivery. Training a 4D Gaussian scene requires multi-view video and significant compute; playback, while real-time on a discrete GPU, has not been trivially portable to the browser. PlayCanvas is a WebGL-based open-source 3D engine designed for exactly that environment: games and interactive experiences that run without plugins. Wiring 4D Gaussian playback into its rendering pipeline means the format inherits the engine's cross-platform reach — desktop, mobile, and headset browsers alike.

The image in the post shows a viewer labelled "Fashion" with an environment selector, hinting that Gracia VR's use case is styled, volumetric video — virtual try-on, lookbooks, or immersive presentations rather than scientific visualisation. That application niche matters: fashion brands are among the few commercial buyers willing to absorb the capture cost of volumetric video today, making them a plausible beachhead for the technology before it scales to broader media.

concepts.definition: A scene-representation method that stores a 3D environment as millions of small, coloured, semi-transparent ellipsoids (Gaussians) learned from photographs. Because the ellipsoids can be sorted and drawn directly by a GPU rasteriser, the method renders in real time — a key advantage over neural radiance fields, which require tracing rays through a neural network for every pixel.

An extension of Gaussian splatting that treats time as a fourth dimension alongside the three spatial ones. Each Gaussian primitive can deform and shift in both space and time, allowing a single learned representation to capture a moving scene. Viewers can then request a rendered frame at any moment without replaying the original video.

The task of generating a photorealistic image of a scene from a camera position and angle that was never photographed. Both NeRFs and Gaussian splatting are trained on multi-view images and then queried to produce views that did not exist in the training set, which is what makes them useful for interactive 3D experiences.

A JavaScript-based 3D graphics framework that targets the WebGL API — a browser-native interface to the device GPU. Applications built on WebGL engines run in any modern browser without plugins, making them accessible on phones, tablets, and headsets as well as desktops.

repos.summary: The official code release for the CVPR 2024 paper "4D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Dynamic Scene Rendering" by the HUST Vision Lab. The repo implements training and evaluation of 4D Gaussian scenes from multi-view video. It is one of two prominent open-source implementations of 4D Gaussian splatting, alongside the Fudan University group's ICLR 2024 release.
